sections.content: This course is an A++ course! If you are new to programming, you can keep up with no problems! Even if you know programming languages beforehand, it is still interesting, as Professor Desmond provides interesting lectures for you to enjoy!
sections.teaching:
Professor Desmond is energetic, considerate, and gives amazing, interactive lectures! You should expect frequent jokes and a perfect pace that you can catch up! Your computational thinking is also trained in the process, preparing you for future programming experiences.
Labs offer some hands-on experience and allow immediate practice after lectures. Labs focus on what you have learned in the most recent lecture, allowing precise practice on your freshly obtained knowledge.
sections.grading: I haven't received a score for this course yet. However, the grading system is very friendly. Your grade is barely affected by your fellow classmates; it's all you! Work hard to earn yourself an A!
sections.workload: The workload for this course is very low, even if you're aiming for an A+. Lectures, facing people who have no prior knowledge, dig through the material at a slow but steady pace. This allows easier reviews and better understanding, making the lab work a piece of sweet sweet cake. If you enjoy programming or wants to figure out if you do, this is the course!

sections.content:
The course splits cleanly into two halves. Before the midterm it covers the standard Python foundations — data types, operators, branching, looping, lists and tuples, dictionaries, and functions. After the midterm it moves into recursion, NumPy, basic OOP, Pandas and Matplotlib.
The pacing between these two halves is uneven. The early lectures move slowly and spend a lot of time on basics, while the libraries at the end are compressed into the final few weeks. NumPy is the pivot of the whole course: it is the hardest topic for most people and also the most heavily examined. Pandas and Matplotlib are covered thinly — Matplotlib has in some semesters been pushed into the labs or left to self-study — yet they still appear in the final.
It is also worth knowing that this is not a gentle "introduction". The course digs into language semantics that beginner tutorials skip: mutability, shallow versus deep copy, short-circuit evaluation, argument passing, name mangling. NumPy in particular is there to prepare you for COMP 2211, so it is not optional knowledge.
sections.teaching:
The teaching is the strongest part of the course. The instructors explain concepts with live demonstrations and a lot of worked examples, and they stay behind after class to answer questions. Lectures are recorded and lecture attendance is not taken, so you can follow along at your own pace if you prefer.
The written materials are unusually good. The course website hosts a large bank of self-test questions and extra practice, which is the single most useful resource for exam preparation. Piazza is answered quickly by both TAs and instructors.
Lab quality varies with the TA you get. Labs are one hour of teaching plus optional Q&A, and attendance is recorded through iPRS, so you do need to show up and answer the questions.
sections.grading:
Grading is relative. The assessed components are lab attendance and lab exercises, two programming assignments, the midterm and the final, with the exams carrying most of the weight.
Labs and PAs are auto-graded on ZINC with unlimited attempts before the deadline, and visible test cases are provided alongside hidden ones. This means full or near-full marks on coursework is achievable for anyone who starts early — and because most of the class does exactly that, coursework barely separates people. Your grade is effectively decided by the two exams.
The exams are handwritten. You write code on paper with no editor, no autocomplete and no error messages, which punishes syntax carelessness in a way the assignments never do. Question design leans toward constrained problems — writing something in a single line, or solving a NumPy task without loops — so knowing a workaround is not enough; you need the specific tool.
One structural point worth knowing: the cohort you sit with matters. Taking this course in the same term as CS and CPEG students means competing against people who already know Python.
sections.workload:
Lab exercises come roughly every other week and are short and reinforcing. The two programming assignments are the real workload. Both come with long specifications and skeleton code that you must read and understand before writing a single line, and that reading often takes longer than the coding. PA2 is noticeably harder than PA1 and leans on OOP and NumPy.

Deadlines are generous, so the workload is manageable if you start early and brutal if you do not. If you have programmed before, the course is light. If you have not, budget several times what you expect, especially after the midterm.

One piece of advice repeated in almost every review, and it is correct: do not let AI write the PAs for you. The assignments are the only sustained coding practice you get, and the exams are handwritten. Debugging your own broken code is the thing that actually prepares you.

sections.content:
he first half of the course is quite basic, covering Python syntax, conditionals, loops, collections and functions. The pace becomes noticeably faster after the midterm when the course moves into recursion, NumPy, Pandas and Matplotlib.

I think the difficulty depends heavily on your programming background. If you have used Python before, most of the first half should be very manageable. For complete beginners, the later topics, especially NumPy and Pandas, may require considerably more practice because they are taught relatively quickly.
sections.teaching:
The teaching is generally very beginner-friendly. Concepts are explained with a lot of examples and the instructors are approachable when students have questions.

One downside is that a lot of lecture time is spent on basic Python concepts, while some of the more useful topics in the second half, particularly NumPy/Pandas/Matplotlib, feel slightly rushed.
sections.grading:
The grading structure is roughly:

Lab: 10%

PA1: 12%

PA2: 13%

Midterm: 25%

Final: 40%

Labs and PAs are quite possible to score highly on if you start early. The assignments provide detailed instructions, skeleton code and visible test cases, so they are not designed to trick you.

However, getting an A-range grade is not necessarily easy because the exams carry 65% of the total grade and there are many students who already have programming experience. Based on the grade distributions mentioned by the instructors, around 20–25% of the class receives an A-range grade while a fairly large proportion receives B-range grades.

So the course is relatively safe if your goal is simply to pass or get a B-range grade, but getting an A requires being comfortably above average in the exams.
sections.workload:
The workload is moderate overall. Labs are usually manageable, while the two PAs can initially look intimidating because the specifications are long and you need some time to understand the existing code before actually implementing anything.

For students with programming experience, the workload should be quite light. For complete beginners, it can be much heavier, especially during the second half of the semester.

Overall, it is a useful introductory Python course and probably easier than it first appears, but I would not call it a free A. The biggest difficulty is not the basic programming itself, but keeping up with the later libraries and performing well enough on the exams to compete for the A range.

Desmond has emphasized to give 25% A range as much as he can
Besides that, the course is also quite competitive as it becomes the required for eng students
Fall term, you need to compete with cs and cpeg and ai program students
Spring term, you need to compete with the rest of eng student AND students from sci school, where the majority of them compete for DSCT etc
To sum up, quite competitive

How to get a good grade based on my own feeling  
1. Play around with VSCode a lot. You can explore on your own while listening to lectures, and you'll find lots of tricky edge cases, etc.  
2. Make good use of existing self-learning resources before the exam. From what I can see, some questions on the 26fall exam clearly point to self-tests (some questions are really weird, but if you've gone through them once before the exam, you'll roughly know how to handle them; very tricky questions won't test pure "principles"—they're basically simple variations of previous questions).  
3. You can find problems online, especially recursion ones.  
Recommended:  
- Top choice: AI-generated problems  
- LeetCode
- Luogu(recommended by others)  
The difficulty of the problems might not be perfect, but the main goal is to look at problems from different backgrounds and practice the core concepts.  
Reminder: In practice, exams won't test those "super hard conceptual" problems; they focus on whether you're familiar with using a few specific methods/variations.

sections.content:
As a local HKDSE student with ICT background (new syllabus),  I think the difficulty of the course is acceptable. Before the mid-term exam, most of the contents have been studied in high school ICT (the whole compulsory part D and 2D array in elective C), so I just re-studied the knowledge I already know before the midterm. However, the mid-term exam is not that easy, better practice more about dealing with indices of Python list (especially 2D array and list compression, some questions ban using looping)  if it is your first time learning Python. After the mid-term, most of the contents are new, the courses focus on studying Numpy function, and I think the concepts is quite abstract. Also, midterm focus on only the functions Python already have, so you have to write the algorithm for the function yourself. But in the final exam, some questions (Numpy, Pandas) ask to directly use the functions in the libraries, you just need to call out the functions correctly in those question to get the point. I think that may be the reason why the average scores of final exam is significantly higher than that of midterm.

I’d say he’s top 10 in all professors I’ve met, but there are things that can be done better.

Good: makes sure you understand, reminds you of details you may not find elsewhere. I do not want to keep saying the good things because you can see it in almost all other reviews, I am here to talk about my honest feelings as a total newbie to programming.

Bad: pretends to focus a lot on exam (more on grading), but not about the content, just about some boring syntax you can totally avoid, forcing us to listen to something that is not useful anywhere outside of this course, just for him to make crazy papers to trick us. (For example when you really write code there are many ways to do something and you can just pick one way that you like, but he forces you to remember the syntax to all the writing methods and may ask you about how to write a program using just one line of code or otherwise 0 marks)

I think for a new programmer, the most important thing is to hone a programming mindset and problem-solving mindset using codes. It is very different whether you can write codes or you can read and understand those codes. I’d say the lecturer spams a lot of codes without giving us sufficient motivation. He basically goes like “Show time” and then show us what happens. He has good explanation only on understand understanding the basic concepts but not on honing problem solving techniques. What I mean is that he always walks through why the program works, but never talks about why the program is designed that way and how to come up with that.

Of course I understand that he gives us a lot of self practice, and we only learn by doing, but it will also be better if experts like him can share more with us about how he approaches questions. (I’m sure he can do it well because he is a good story teller, nothing can be easier than just walking through what he has in mind with us) When the focus is about explaining why the program works, it is not really worth it to take lessons because I can just read the notes and run through it line by line (the notes are made by him too, and are good enough to a level that can replace him…), I think insights and thinking are much more precious and should be emphasised a lot more.

I believe this is important, especially for an introductory course (for courses like COMP 2711H, professor never talks about problem-solving and only discusses the beauty of the theorem and the intuition, that is totally fine because it is not an introductory course and we can learn about doing on our own, I am just claiming that it is not appropriate for the very first course in anything like programming)
sections.grading:
Mid term:
The most terrible mid term exam I’ve ever had, even crazier than real analysis, HHM’s multivariable calculus or anything. First, if you need to think, then you won’t be able to finish the paper. Secondly, if you need time to understand their instructions, you won’t be able to finish the paper. Thirdly, if you will be careless under time constraints, I can guarantee you that the number of mistakes you will make in this paper will be much greater than what you do for other paper.
Basically, what is tested has absolutely nothing to do with what is taught. The whole paper is an IQ test about programming, I can guarantee you that it has very little to do with how hard-working you are, as the sole purpose of the paper is just to give you a hard time.
For the T/F questions, some questions are out of syllabus and the concepts were never mentioned in any occasions, nor are they important, whether you know them or not has nothing to do with whether you are a good programmer.
And then the next question asks us to implement them line by line, excuse me, why don’t you just ask us the final output? What’s the point?
And the long questions were basically disaster, they forced you to use particular methods by limiting your number of lines to the answers, which is so stupid because a key part of programming is about algorithmic creativity, his practice of limiting our creativity is extremely discouraging and inappropriate for any purpose as an introductory programming course. Also, the number of questions and reading we need to do exceeded a normal time limit outrageously, come on it is not 2012H, it’s so pointless that the mean last year is 55 and they probably think it’s not low enough and decided to add two more questions to our paper, and of course our paper was much harder than last semester as well, which makes it extremely devastating to even take the exam. It is definitely the worst midterm I have ever taken.
Note: the reason why I say he pretends to focus on exam is that he always say “in the exam I can ask you …”, but he actually never does. All he asks are the Demon questions that anre extremely hard to come up with as an intro, and he has never offered any clues to help us with the exam. All he says is the basics of the basics and won’t help you get more than 30 marks in the exam.
To be honest I understand why he does this because so many people are already experienced and he does not want to make the paper too easy so those people get full marks easily, but he fails to accommodate major students’ needs and tricking us and showing off and telling us how weak we are become his whole purpose given the ratio of demon questions and terrible time constraint. This is pure nonsense

Final:
Somehow this paper is much more doable than the mid term paper. First of all, the comprehension part was not overly complicated so it would be find if you took the time to read. Secondly, the number of questions is just mid term + 1 and we have 1 more hour to do, making it manageable. However, the questions are still pretty hard and I believe some of them are out of our ability if the only assumed knowledge is comp 1023. For example, the final numpy question requires some basic linear algebra computation knowledge which was not stated as a prerequisite of this course, making it hard to do. Next, the recursion question was 2711 level and requires 3 base cases, but the lecturer never mentioned more than 1 base case, making it quite impossible to think of the solution under the first exposure. (Turned out it did have a solution with 1 base case only but that’s almost impossible to think about). Also, 20 marks about OOP is non sense (it’s not hard tho) as he literally only gave 1 lecture about OOP. Anyway, it seems that they expect us to be very experienced programmer by taking this course, which is really hard in 3 month time. Comp 1023 is never easy, and it’s way harder than 1021, I believe the difficulty is similar to 2011 (excluding pointer), so good luck. Also, this paper gives a vibe that “CS is not someone anyone can do by grinding”, it takes some ingenuity, which I think is quite discouraging for pure CS ppl (for CS + Math talents, you probably get A+ or A easily).

sections.content:
The title of this course is kind of a scam. This really isn't an "introduction" to python programming. If this is your first time programming, I highly suggest to drop this course and take COMP 1021 + 1028 instead to fulfill the requirements.

The content covers your standard topics of python and programming such as control flow, conditional logic, loops, data types etc. It then covers some data analysis libraries i.e. numpy, pandas and matplotlib which are useful if you are going to take AI courses in the future.

However, personally, I think some of the content chosen is of a very poor standard for an introduction course. I feel like recursion as well as the data analysis libraries aren't really very beginner level concepts. In fact, I felt some useful content such as exception handling, string manipulation, file handling etc. were left out which is much more essential than something like matplotlib for e.g.

Also pandas and matplotlib might as well have not been in the syllabus because barely anything was covered for them. It was basically a "just read the documentation bro" chapter and that's how the exam questions were set from it as well.
sections.teaching:
I did not attend a single lecture because they were boring as fuck if you already knew python well. Also I just find it much faster to read the notes and practice yourself than attend lectures but that's just my preference.

However, I did attend the labs (cuz mandatory attendance) and I'll say that the teaching was fucking dogshit, not cuz the TAs couldn't teach, but cuz of what they actually taught. As beginners, I think it is much more important to focus on how to use programming concepts to solve problems rather than focusing on how they work in depth. Yet all the lab quizzes tested dumbass knowledge like what the output of a confusing bundle of if-statements should be etc. This was useful for me, as a programmer with a solid python background, as it solidified my understanding of python as a programming language, but if you never coded before, this is just useless knowledge.

The self tests suffered from the same issues, they just tested in depth internal working of python code, not how to write python code to solve specific problems. At least the uploaded some practice problems, but that was like only 1 week before the final exam. They should have uploaded those problems way before; I think that would have helped the true beginners a lot more.

I personally haven't approached him to ask any questions, but judging by how I often see him talking to students, he's very willing to help if you run into any problems. The anonymous Piazza forum on Canvas also allows you to ask questions if you don't like talking to people face-to-face.

sections.content:
1. Introduction to Computing and Programming Basics
   Overview of computers, basic programming concepts, and the purpose of programming languages.

2. Core Python Fundamentals
   - Basic built-in data types (int, float, str, bool, None)
   - Essential operators: arithmetic (+ − * /), assignment, comparison, logical (and, or, not)
   - Short-circuit (lazy) evaluation in and / or expressions
   - Small integer caching / interning behavior

3. Decision Making – Conditional Execution
   - if, elif, else statements
   - Structural pattern matching with match … case

4. Repetition – Loops
   - for loops (including iteration over sequences)
   - while loops
   - Loop control: break, continue, else clause on loops

5. Container / Collection Data Types
   - Sequences: list and tuple – creation, methods, operators, slicing
   - Shallow copy vs deep copy (especially with nested structures)
   - Dictionaries: creation, access, modification, common operations, dictionary views

6. Code Organization I – Functions & Recursion
   - Defining functions, parameters, return values
   - Type hints / function annotations
   - Positional arguments, keyword arguments, default values
   - Variable scope: local vs global (global / nonlocal keywords)
   - Passing mutable vs immutable objects to functions
   - Recursion: base case, recursive case, call stack behavior

7. Code Organization II – Modules, Packages & Functional Tools
   - Creating and importing modules
   - Packages and the role of __init__.py
   - Lambda (anonymous) functions
   - Higher-order functions: map(), filter()

8. Object-Oriented Programming in Python
   - Defining classes and creating instances
   - Instance variables and methods
   - public and "private" naming conventions
   - Name mangling (__variable) and its purpose

9. Python Library – NumPy, Pandas and Matplotlib
   - NumPy basics: ndarrays, vectorized operations, shape, axes, broadcasting
   - Very basic Pandas: Series, DataFrame, simple selection and filtering
   - Minimal Matplotlib: line plots, scatter plots, basic figure customization(Taught in tutorial)

The course taught basic python concepts: types, control flow, functions, collections, classes, etc, coupled with introduction to popular python packages (numpy, pandas, and matplotlib).

The problematic part was the python packages: each (of three!) have their own quirks and mechanisms (e.g. numpy's indexing and broadcasting) that has nothing to do those previously learnt python concepts. sections.content: The course content is well-structured and starts from the absolute basics, making it truly accessible for beginners. It systematically progresses to more complex topics. While the concepts themselves are not inherently "hard," the pace can be challenging as it requires quick assimilation and consistent practice to keep up.
sections.teaching: The teaching quality is a highlight of the course. Instructors are typically clear, engaging, and supportive. They explain concepts thoroughly and are responsive to questions during lectures and office hours. The use of practical examples helps solidify theoretical understanding.
sections.grading: The grading scheme is generally considered fair and lenient in terms of marking criteria. However, the course curve can feel intense due to the presence of many highly skilled students (including those with prior programming experience or exceptional aptitude). For a true beginner, achieving a top grade requires significant effort and proactive learning.
sections.workload: The workload is substantial. It includes regular programming assignments, quizzes, lab work, and a final project. Some assignments, particularly those involving integrated concepts or external libraries (like numpy which is crazy hard for beginners), can be difficult for beginners, demanding considerable time for research, trial-and-error, and debugging.

sections.grading:
The course uses "relative grading". (according to unofficial data, around 70% of students get B-A range)

Lab(including attendance(all labs) and exercise x4 out of 5)
PA(programme assignment)x2
Mid-term
Final

Both Labs and PAs provide shown test cases(50%) and skeleton codes, so it is possible to understand what it requires u to finish. There are also 50% of hidden test cases to ensure ur code is reasonable instead of by luck or hard coding. Both of them provide unlimited attempts before deadlines so u can try as many times as possible to get at least 50% marks. They do take u time to understand and finish so finish them asap is recommended. For Labs, PA1 and PA2, I got 100%, 95% and 100% respectively. So they are possible for beginners like me to finish those assignments.

Since the contents for mid-term are covered in secondary school, I found that it is impossible for me to be above upper quartile. Yet, having the new topic numpy, most ppl learnt from the beginning like me. Listening to lecturer's teaching and asking tas questions, I was above the upper quartile in the final.

The exam curve might seem to be terrifying, but it is possible for beginners to get a good grade. I got an A- in this course which was out of expectation.

sections.content:
No turtle anymore

1. Introduction to Computers and Programming
2. Python Programming Fundamentals
- fundamental data types, mutable objects and immutable objects
- fundamental operators like +, -, *, /, assignment operators and logic operators
- short circuiting/lazy operation of and, or
- caches of small integers
3. Branching Statements
- if statements
- match case statements
4. Looping Statements
- for and while
5. Collections – container data types
- list and tuple, and their operators, slicing
- deep copy and shallow copy in list
- nature of list and tuple: list are mutable, tuple are immutable
- dict and their operator, immutable keys
- list/tuple/dict comprehension (useful for one-liners)
6. Modularization – Functions and Recursions
- functions, type hint, positional argument and keyword argument
- global variables
- passing mutable object to functions
- recursions
7. Modularization - Modules, Packages, and Libraries
- functional programming using reduce, map, filter functions
- lambda functions
8. Object-Oriented Programming
- use of class and their "public", "private", "protected" members, name mangling
9. NumPy, Pandas and Matplotlib
- NumPy, their operations and properties, and broadcasting, fancy indexing, slicing
- introduced very minimal Pandas and Matplotlib

PS: Talking about the notorious NumPy, it seems to be included to connect the content of COMP2211, so if you don't plan to take COMP2211 in your later semesters, it's quite natural to think that module is useless, but whatever this course tries to provide a smooth transition to COMP2211 and that's the aim of this course, so I won't say sth like teaching this module in this course is bad, but it's true that this course's content and schedule are quite immature, with a rush teaching in numpy and shift quite a long time in teaching basic syntaxes. I believe the details of its immaturity is being emphasized a lot in many other reviews.

PS: Some people are just complaining the limitation of prohibiting the use of for, while loops in NumPy question. I would say if for, while loops are not prohibited, there is no means to introduce NumPy to reduce the running time, so only allows using NumPy functions and limiting the use of loops is reasonable to encourage you to understand NumPy arrays more, but not treating it as another version of nested lists....

sections.workload:
As a introductory cs major course, the workload of this course is quite fair.
Lab exercises do not require a lot of times to finish, while for PA1 and PA2, I used 1.5 hours and 4 hours respectively to finish.

Midterm is an exam emphasizes hand-writing code (and some problems requires you to write in oneline) so for some people who are new to programming, this exam will be a bit rush and difficult.
While Final exam shifts its majority question types to ask the output of some codes, fill in the blanks on a semi-finished code, and some questions asking you where is the error, which is similar to COMP1021. However, the coding part still take a large portion (~55%?) in the exam paper and NumPy questions are quite hard, so I recommend you to take Python Proficiency Test first to have a look of those question types and put more efforts on practicing NumPy.
